title: El Bola
full_review:
A Madrid boy's friendship with a new classmate helps save his life in the wrenching drama "El Bola" (Film Movement).

Twelve-year-old Pablo (Juan Jose Ballesta) is seen at the railroad tracks with schoolmates who play a dangerous game of jumping off the tracks just before the train hurtles by. But he is in equal danger at home, where his volatile father (Manuel Moron) beats him at the slightest provocation, ignoring his wife's protests to stop.

When Alfredo (Pablo Galan) joins his class, insecure Pablo shyly befriends the more confident boy. But he keeps secret the shame of a father who brutalizes him, implying he will never measure up to another son who died in a car crash.

Visiting Alfredo at his home, Pablo is exposed to the kind of family he has never known. Alfredo's mom and toddler brother welcome Pablo into their midst as does dad Jose (Alberto Gimenez), who operates a tattoo parlor. Several of Jose's friends are gay and one, Alfredo's godfather, is dying of AIDS.

After Alfredo's family includes Pablo on a day trip, Pablo's furious father attacks him and warns he must never again associate with Alfredo or his family.

When the curious Alfredo wonders why his pal is out of school so long and visits his apartment when the boy is alone, there is no disguising the boy's bruised face and body.

Alfredo tells his parents who decide to get involved, especially when Pablo escapes and goes to them. But first they learn that the law may see them as kidnappers and that social services has no easy answers.

Writer-director Achero Manas' feature debut wisely avoids sentimentality yet packs an emotional punch. However, it's not easy to watch the enraged father slugging and viciously beating his son -- who, naturally, grows to hate his father. Through his new friendship and the support of a loving family, Pablo is able to confront his fears and stand a chance at a normal life.

The drama is less successful in indicating why Pablo's father is such a monster, and blaming his rage or grief over the lost son is only vaguely suggested. The deliberate pacing, however, allows a credible friendship to develop between the two pre-teen boys as well as the peaceful atmosphere in Alfredo's home, which is in sharp contrast to the misery and tension in Pablo's apartment.

The film cries out for teachers, friends, neighbors and relatives not to ignore youngsters they suspect may be in an abusive situation but are too afraid to speak out.

With its realistic and understated performances, "El Bola" makes important points and director Manas should earn the respect of his peers and the opportunity to again address social issues in this medium.

Subtitles.

Due to brutal violence to a minor, fleeting nude female images, some rough language, occasional crude expressions and an instance of profanity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. Not rated by the Motion Picture Association of America.
